title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service used for recording virtual meetings is facing legal claims that it recorded conversations without participant consent and used those recordings to train its AI systems. The lawsuit alleges that the default recording behavior and the consent mechanism did not adequately inform users, particularly regarding how their data would be used. It is not established whether the company's stated privacy policy actually did grant explicit permission through a checkbox, whether participants read or understood it, or whether the allegations have merit.

The failure occurred in the deployment of a system that collected voice data from meetings across multiple platforms without requiring affirmative consent from all participants at the point of recording. Catching this would have required either obtaining explicit opt-in consent from every meeting participant before recording began, or designing the system to record only when all parties had actively confirmed participation in data collection. The company's reliance on a privacy policy checkbox does not establish that users understood what data would be collected or how it would be used.

Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations
Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed Friday accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View company that provides AI-powered transcription services, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit, brought by Justin Brewer of San Jacinto, California, claims the company's Otter Notebook service records virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without alerting participants that recordings will be used to train its artificial intelligence systems. The lawsuit alleges this practice violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and is done to generate financial gain.

Otter claims its privacy policy grants users explicit permission to use meeting transcripts for AI training when they check a box, but the lawsuit argues many people are still deceived. The company serves approximately 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since its 2016 founding. Recent complaints on social media have highlighted instances where automated recordings backfired, including an incident where confidential business details were shared after a participant left a meeting. The lawsuit questions whether Otter's method of anonymizing conversation data effectively removes confidential information or protects speaker identity.
